newsitem.title: GERMANY: Local job deals won't ease German labour costs.
newsitem.headline: Local job deals won't ease German labour costs.

text.p: Special agreements that have allowed a few German companies to cut costs at individual plants were unlikely to spark widespread change in Germany's hamstrung labour market, economists said on Monday.

A pact at a Mercedes-Benz AG bus plant last week appeared to present the kind of solution that could preserve jobs and revitalise German competitiveness while unemployment stood at its highest level since the Great Depression.

But such one-time agreements were out of reach for all but the largest of companies, and failed to fix the structural weaknesses of the German labour market, said Werner Verbockett, a Commerzbank AG economist in Frankfurt.

"We have seen these types of agreements in the past and they don't really affect a lot of mid-sized businesses," Verbockett told Reuters. "Auto makers have had agreements for specific locations for a long time and that hasn't made the auto labour market more flexible."
But Verbockett doubted added flexibility for individual plants would have a broad impact on the 4.66 million unemployed Germany reported in January.

"Half of all the unemployed are not skilled workers. Education is a problem," he said. Reduced break time and leaves of absence would have little impact on the wage and sick pay levels that push German labour costs above most other countries', Verbockett said.

Workers at Mercedes' Mannheim plant agreed to reduced break and sick time in exchange for management's agreement to forego layoffs and reduce the payroll only through attrition until at least the end of 2000. Mercedes also said Mannheim workers could take leaves of absence of six months to three years.

The concessions were allowed under the leeway permitted in industry-wide union contracts, plant spokesman Norbert Burchard told Reuters. Mercedes has used similar agreements to cut costs at Sindelfingen, Bremen and Kassel facilities.
"The Mannheim location wouldn't have closed without this agreement, but it could only be competitive if we reduced costs considerably," he said. "The agreement lets us do that."

The Mercedes pact came two days after conglomerate workers at the medical technology unit of Siemens AG agreed to a job-cutting plan. The unit would cut 1,200 jobs -- half through early retirement, severance packages or transfers -- in exchange for investments to raise productivity.
Siemens chief Heinrich von Pierer, in the daily Die Welt on Monday, said further leeway was urgently needed in union pacts.

Contract negotiators "have it extraordinarily difficult because they must bring big companies and mid-sized companies under one roof. Also export-oriented companies and those that only sell in their own country," von Pierer said. "That's why I would like industry-wide contracts to be reformed."
Steel maker Krupp Hoesch Stahl AG last week also reached a deal with workers to extend the life of a Dortmund plant in exchange for cutting 2,200 of its 10,000 jobs through attrition and divestment.
